name: Jump rope
lead: A jump rope, or skipping rope, is a cord with a handle at each end that is swung under the feet and over the head while the user jumps. It is used recreationally, in fitness programmes, in combat-sport training and in organised competition, with freestyle and speed events overseen internationally by the International Jump Rope Union [1].

Skipping is classed as aerobic exercise comparable to running or cycling at moderate to vigorous intensity [1]. It is inexpensive and portable, and in looksmaxxing and fitness communities it is associated with conditioning, calf endurance and staying lean.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 trials involving 1,021 mostly young participants reported improvements in resting heart rate, body mass index, fat mass, cardiorespiratory endurance, strength, jumping, range of motion and sprinting, with no significant effects on blood pressure, waist-hip circumference, bone or lean mass [2]. Most participants in this research were younger than 18, so the findings do not directly describe adult physique outcomes [2].

paras: Speed ropes use a thin vinyl cord or wire and are intended for fast jumping and double-unders, and they wear quickly on rough surfaces such as concrete [1]. Licorice ropes are made from flexible vinyl or PVC and are common in freestyle [1]. Beaded ropes produce audible feedback when the beads strike the floor and are used in rhythmic skipping and double Dutch [1]. Leather ropes are thicker, less prone to tangling and wear more slowly outdoors [1]. Weighted ropes increase resistance, and with it difficulty [1].

Rope jumping has a long and multicultural history. Wikipedia reports evidence from Han-dynasty China, where it was linked to New Year celebrations, and from ancient Egypt, where children are depicted jumping over vines [1]. Explorers recorded vine-jumping among Indigenous Australians in the 16th century [1]. In Europe and North America, it was initially mostly a boys' activity in the 16th and 17th centuries and became popular among girls from the 18th century [1].

In the 20th century it became a staple of boxing and other combat-sport training, and one source names Jack Dempsey among early boxers who used it [3]. The sport is now organised internationally, with a world championship held in Kawasaki, Japan, in 2025 [1][3]. Skipping gained popularity as a space-efficient home workout during the COVID-19 pandemic [1]. Details drawn from the machine-written source have not been verified against primary histories.

Repeated low jumps load the calves, feet and lower legs rhythmically, raise heart rate quickly, and require coordination between hands and feet [1]. A study published in Gait & Posture in 2019, cited by Wikipedia, reported that skipping produced lower knee contact forces than running [1]. A 2014 study examined whether jump-rope work could serve as stretch-shortening cycle training [4], and a 2020 study in endurance runners linked jump-rope training to better 3-km time-trial performance through greater lower-limb reactivity and foot-arch stiffness [5].

The 2022 meta-analysis of jump rope training lasting 6 to 40 weeks reported effect sizes from small to large on fitness outcomes in healthy young participants [2]. A 2023 meta-analysis of 15 studies in 10- to 12-year-olds found that jumping rope did not show a significant advantage over regular physical education for body morphology, while reporting subgroup improvements in fitness measures such as speed, strength and endurance in boys and resting heart rate in girls [6].
Evidence for calf size specifically is limited. The studies above measure endurance, jumping and body composition, and did not report calf muscle growth as an outcome in the abstracts available.

Overuse injuries of the calf, shin and Achilles tendon are commonly reported by trainers among beginners who increase volume quickly, and landing repeatedly on hard surfaces loads the joints. A study of footwear selection for jump rope examined how different shoes change lower-extremity biomechanics [7]. Skipping is described as producing lower knee joint forces than running in one study [1].

A 2022 meta-analysis pooled 21 trials in healthy young participants [2], and a 2023 meta-analysis pooled 15 trials in preadolescents [6]. In a 2025 randomized trial of 120 overweight or obese adolescents aged 10 to 13, a 12-week interval jump rope programme in physical education was tested against no training for body composition, fitness and glycolipid metabolism [8]. Smaller randomized trials in obese adolescent girls and boys have examined body composition and insulin sensitivity after 12 weeks of jump rope exercise [9][10], and a trial in adolescent girls with prehypertension examined abdominal adiposity and vascular function [11]. Trials in athletes include an 8-week combined jump-rope and elastic-band programme in young basketball players, which improved agility, balance and sprint times [12]. Adult-specific trials focused on appearance outcomes were not found.

In appearance-focused communities, jump rope is discussed as a cheap conditioning tool for staying lean and training footwork and calf endurance. Online communities dedicated to jump rope focus on technique, rope selection and freestyle skills. Specific claims about calf growth or fat loss are generally framed as lore rather than as demonstrated outcomes.

timeline.event: Two US rope-skipping organisations merge to form the United States Amateur Jump Rope Federation, later renamed USA Jump Rope [1].
The International Jump Rope Union receives observer status from the international sports federation body GAISF [1].
Skipping gains popularity as a home workout during COVID-19 lockdowns [1].
The IJRU's second world tournament is held in Kawasaki, Japan [1].
